We model this trade-off as a game in which nodes choose how to mix their own representations with strict-neighborhood aggregates. For fixed channel representations, task supervision defines a common-payoff game, while local distinctness payoffs induce an exact potential game whose potential is the degree-normalized strict Dirichlet energy. We introduce CG2, which amortizes these choices through a shared six-parameter policy per layer based on local channel statistics and can be trained using either objective. Controlled comparisons show that the shared task-trained policy improves mean performance over fixed mixing on three of five heterophily benchmarks, with significant gains on two, while free per-node actions trained with either objective rarely improve on the same baseline. On the ECHO long-range benchmark, the clearest contribution of the gate appears on eccentricity, where the task-trained policy substantially reduces prediction error.

papers.title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference
papers.summary: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.

papers.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
papers.summary: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.

papers.title: NeuroMotion: Aligning EEG to Discrete Motion Primitives for Continuous Motion Decoding
papers.summary: EEG-to-motion decoding remains challenging because noisy scalp EEG is difficult to map directly to continuous kinematics. We present NeuroMotion, a framework that aligns EEG representations to discrete motion primitives for continuous motion decoding across heterogeneous paradigms, including full-body free movement, lower-limb treadmill locomotion, and upper-limb freewill reaching and grasping. A VQ-based motion prior discretizes continuous motion into reusable primitives that serve as both alignment prototypes and intermediate prediction targets. Prototypical and supervised contrastive objectives align EEG embeddings to motion-derived prototypes and organize them according to primitive assignments. An E2M Transformer predicts motion-code sequences from the learned EEG representations, while a final geometric refinement stage improves continuous trajectory reconstruction through motion-level training. Under a last-session test protocol, NeuroMotion achieves the best mean reconstruction performance among the compared EEG decoding baselines across all three datasets, with the clearest gains on full-body motion in both reconstruction accuracy and distribution-level quality. Multi-subject ablations further support the contributions of EEG-to-primitive alignment, token prediction, and refinement. Code is available at https://github.com/Liuyi2351433/NeuroAction.

papers.title: Precise Asymptotics of Non-Convex M-Estimators
papers.summary: Precise asymptotic theory for M-estimators in high-dimensional settings is largely limited to convex or mildly non-convex formulations, yet non-convex loss functions as well as regularizers are widely used in practice. We study M-estimation in generalized linear models (GLMs) where the loss function or the regularizer can be non-convex. Under rotationally invariant design matrices in the proportional asymptotic regime, we analyze the problem through Vector Approximate Message Passing (VAMP), whose iterates are described by a low-dimensional deterministic recursion called State Evolution (SE). Existing proofs of SE require the proximal operators of the loss function and the regularizer to be Lipschitz, but a non-convex loss or regularizer can have a discontinuous proximal operator, and the usual Onsager terms in VAMP then miss the contribution of the discontinuities. Assuming that the proximal operators are special functions of locally bounded variation, we derive a correction to the Onsager terms using a distributional Stein's lemma. We prove that SE holds for the corrected VAMP. We apply the theory to analyze group sparse regression with an $\ell_0$-type penalty and to robust regression with the Cauchy loss.

papers.title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation
papers.summary: Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

papers.title: PVFormer: Proper Velocity Transformer for Stable and Scalable Hyperbolic Representation Learning
papers.summary: Hyperbolic representations have shown remarkable success on hierarchical and tree-like data, and Transformers have become a central architecture for representation learning. However, a principled construction of hyperbolic Transformers remains challenging because the self-attention layer decomposes into three coupled primitives, transformation, similarity, and aggregation, that should all respect the underlying geometry. Existing hyperbolic Transformer designs are typically built in the Poincaré or Lorentz models, where bounded domains, time-like constraints, tangent-space detours, or projection steps make it difficult to keep the full block intrinsic and scalable. To address this gap, we propose PVFormer, to the best of our knowledge, the first Transformer architecture that operates natively in proper velocity (PV) space. The proper velocity model provides an unconstrained representation of hyperbolic geometry, and PVFormer exploits this structure to redesign the Transformer block in PV space. On the transformation side, we use PV homomorphism transformations to update query and value representations. On the similarity side, we generalize Euclidean inner-product attention with a PV Busemann score inspired by Busemann-based hyperbolic learning and a PV point-to-hyperplane key transformation. On the aggregation side, we replace Euclidean averaging with PV midpoint aggregation and further derive a scalable PV linear attention variant for large graphs. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of PVFormer across graph, text, and vision benchmarks.

papers.title: Reconstructing 3D+t Cardiovascular Flow From Sparse Planar Velocity Fields With Neural Fields
papers.summary: Reconstructing time-resolved three-dimensional (3D+t) cardiovascular flow from sparse planar measurements is challenging because each plane observes only the two in-plane velocity components, on a small part of the volume. We propose a plane-aware neural-field framework that learns a continuous 3D velocity field from space and time coordinates through a per-plane projection, and then investigate the potential benefits of physics constraints. We evaluate the framework on computational aortic and aneurysm datasets, and on planes resampled from a real cardiac 4D Flow MRI scan. A plain multi-layer perceptron (MLP) was more accurate than classical radial basis function (RBF) interpolation on both computational datasets. For the aorta, a physics-constrained SIREN (PC-SIREN) reduced the rRMSE further to $0.3756$, compared with $0.4273$ for the plain MLP and $0.7256$ for RBF, and it was the most accurate model in every anatomical segment of the MRI data. For the aneurysms the plain MLP remained the most accurate model, with an rRMSE of $0.07$ to $0.16$ against $0.55$ to $0.71$ for PC-SIREN. Further experiments investigated scanning configuration, number of scans, and spatial resolution. These findings show that continuous neural fields can reconstruct volumetric cardiovascular flow from sparse planar measurements, and that physics constraints have to be matched to the flow.

papers.title: Object-Centric Differentiable Logic Networks for Abstract Visual Reasoning
papers.summary: Human visual intelligence enables efficient reasoning capabilities on abstract visual problems with bounded cognitive resources and minimal experience, and yields remarkable generalization to novel problems with its ability to draw relational analogies and modular abstractions. In contrast, deep learning models require exhaustive task-specific training on large datasets, making them prone to exploiting visual shortcuts and resulting in poor generalization. While neuro-symbolic approaches attempt to bridge this gap by decoupling perception from reasoning with dedicated computation units, existing solutions rely either on explicit rule supervision or parameter-heavy transformer architectures that reintroduce the computational inefficiencies they aim to solve. We introduce Slot-Dwn to address these limitations, a novel neuro-symbolic architecture that unifies unsupervised object-centric perception with logic-based symbolic reasoning. Our model utilizes a Multi-Head Differentiable Weightless Network (MH-DWN) that performs efficient reasoning entirely in Boolean space using look-up tables (LUTs). Our framework reduces visual perception complexity and introduces a LUT-based relational bottleneck with sparse input routing to minimize computational overhead. We evaluate Slot-Dwn across various abstract visual reasoning benchmark tasks targeting systematic rule generalization, sample-efficient anomaly detection, and multi-relational reasoning. We demonstrate that Slot-Dwn yields competitive performance with respect to the state-of-the-art, under extreme out-of-distribution regimes, while requiring up to 52% fewer trainable parameters, with significantly faster convergence.

papers.title: Bridging Continuous-Time MAPF and Industrial AGV Fleet Coordination with Lazy Priority-Based Search
papers.summary: Continuous-time multi-agent path finding on roadmaps (MAPF$_R$) offers a principled way to coordinate robot fleets with geometric collision avoidance, yet its deployment on industrial automated guided vehicle (AGV) infrastructures remains challenging, as highly connected and redundant roadmaps amplify both safe-interval reasoning and multi-agent interaction handling. To bridge this gap, we formalize AGV-MAPF$_R$-CTC, a configuration-space variant of MAPF$_R$ with precomputed continuous-time conflicts that enables the reuse of MAPF$_R$ solvers for AGV fleet coordination with minimal changes. We then revisit continuous-time priority-based search (CPBS), identifying the boundary conditions required by its safe interval path planning (SIPP) low-level planner under priority-induced constraints and enabling earlier solution detection. As a central contribution, we analyze the structure of the priority search space, clarifying which agents are affected by each priority refinement and when replanning can be avoided. Building on this analysis, we introduce a novel algorithm, Lazy-CPBS, which materializes high-level nodes lazily: a child's plans are computed only when it is expanded, so siblings that are never expanded cost no low-level search. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks and on industrial AGV roadmaps imported from a proprietary digital-twin simulator show that CPBS-based solvers remain effective well beyond the agent counts reachable by optimal MAPF$_R$ solvers, while Lazy-CPBS substantially reduces CPBS overhead and offers the most consistent robustness/runtime trade-off across industrial layouts.

papers.title: From joint attention to shared symbols: A free-energy principle account
papers.summary: Joint attention precedes vocabulary acquisition. How can attending to the same object help two people with different sensory experiences come to use a shared word? In a free-energy principle account, marginalizing the common object induces a statistical dependence between private perceptual states. In a categorical world, the joint prior inherits a mixture structure whose component index provides a candidate for shared reference. The collective predictive coding model approximates this prior by representing the dependence through that shared index. An established Metropolis-Hastings naming game lets agents infer and exchange words using private evidence. Toy and multiview image experiments illustrate how word exchange can coordinate private categories and improve the fit of collective models. The account connects joint attention to shared symbols through the coupling of private inference.

papers.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
papers.summary: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.

papers.title: Causal Evidence for the Emergence and Spread of Reward Hacking in AI Agent Swarms
papers.summary: Autonomous AI agents that coordinate and collaborate among each other have become pervasive across domains ranging from scientific research to finance and engineering. The opportunity to share messages and build upon each other's work also creates the potential for misaligned behaviors to spread across AI agents. We provide causal evidence that mere exposure to reward hacking, cheating on a task to pass an automated check, is enough to spread the behavior among AI agents, even after the cheat has been rejected. We conducted 17 preregistered experiments with six frontier models (n = 20,111 agents). First, we show that cheating emerges spontaneously. When agents were told that work passing the visible tests is accepted, 33% cheated in the first round, when the shared record of teammates' submissions was empty. Second, we show that agents who rarely cheat when working alone cheat most of the time after seeing a teammate's cheat, as 94% of teammates who saw an accepted cheat cheated. Third, we show that rejection of reward-hacked solutions offers little protection, using experiments that changed only the label on the cheat. Most agents copied a cheat labeled rejected, 34% of agents cheated after an AI reviewer had rejected the cheat, and nearly every agent copied a cheat labeled accepted. Fourth, we show that cheating generalizes to new tasks. On a new problem with an empty collaboration record, 70% of agents who had earlier seen an accepted cheat cheated again, compared with 32% of agents who had seen an empty record. Fifth, we show that cheating spreads from neighbor to neighbor through networks of 256 agents. In the networks, 44% of agents with a cheating neighbor cheated, compared with 2% of other agents. Together, the results suggest that mere exposure can spread misaligned behavior among AI agents, and that catching a cheat is insufficient once other agents have seen the cheat.

papers.title: TRAE: Trustworthy Automated ESG Annotation via Multi-Agent Consensus and Confidence Assessment
papers.summary: With the growing demand for ESG disclosure and evaluation, constructing high-quality datasets for automatically extracting ESG-related information from large-scale documents has become essential. However, ESG annotation remains challenging due to strong context dependence, ambiguous label boundaries, and the need for domain expertise, resulting in high annotation cost and limited scalability. To address these challenges, we propose TRAE (TRustworthy Automated ESG annotation), a multi-agent framework for scalable and reliable ESG data construction. Unlike direct LLM-based annotation, TRAE evaluates annotation reliability by modeling agreement, confidence, and reasoning consistency among multiple agents through a structured multi-step reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that TRAE improves annotation performance compared with existing automated annotation strategies. Furthermore, TRAE supports a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy that assigns expert labeling only to uncertain samples, reducing annotation cost while preserving data quality. Using TRAE, we construct a high-quality ESG dataset containing approximately 20,000 instances with complete reasoning traces, intermediate agent outputs, and reliability information to enhance transparency and reproducibility. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable framework for trustworthy ESG data construction. The code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/nowzer0/TRAE.

papers.title: Notes on Generative AI for Mathematical Research
papers.summary: These notes describe how generative AI is now used to solve and to check research-level mathematics, with a focus on agents and their harnesses. For the proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and the verification agent OSVerify, we explain the design principles, compare each with its base model, present case studies, and show how to use and contribute to them. We also briefly review the history of AI for mathematics and the community's reactions to it.

papers.title: AEP:Towards Trustworthy Agent Communication, Networking, and Collaboration
papers.summary: As privately owned agents become increasingly capable, collaboration in open agent networks is limited by partial topology knowledge, ownership boundaries, and the risk of exposing or contaminating private context. Existing agent-to-agent protocols are useful when collaborators are already known, while shared-memory and broadcast-based systems rely on visibility and trust assumptions that do not hold in decentralized, low-trust environments. We introduce Open Private Agent Collaboration (OPAC), an asset-centric paradigm for cooperation among private agents with open membership, partial observability, and ownership-aware access control. Rather than treating collaboration as the exchange of final responses, OPAC enables agents to selectively discover, exchange, audit, and integrate policy-controlled context assets. This shifts the unit of cooperation from transient messages to reusable external context, while keeping disclosure and integration subject to privacy and security constraints. We instantiate OPAC with the Agent Exchange Protocol (AEP), a decentralized framework that combines semantic discovery, demand-driven coordination, safety-gated asset exchange, and ledger-backed evidence derivation. By distinguishing physical topology from each agent's local cognitive topology, AEP allows agents to discover task-conditioned collaborators under an unknown network structure, release only admissible assets, and update future cooperation decisions from auditable interaction evidence. AEP therefore provides a middle ground between pure request-response interaction and globally shared memory, offering a practical foundation for trustworthy agent-native networking through selective, auditable reuse of distributed context assets.

papers.title: Social Interaction Breaks Replicate Independence in Controlled-Clone LLM Agents
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM evaluations and social simulations create many agents from one model and treat them as independent replicates, even after the agents interact. This assumption remains untested with matched controls. We introduce SocCogEval, a controlled-clone assay for Social Cognitive Transfer (SCT). Clones share the base model, system prompt, and decoding parameters and differ only in a private brief, and a factorial protocol separates the brief, 30 rounds of interaction, and initialization noise. On Qwen3-122B-FP8, interaction with the briefs held fixed raises off-topic BFI-10 response-profile drift by $\barΔ=+0.917$ and $+0.912$ in two topically disjoint scenarios (exact $p=0.0008$ and $0.0039$). The drift is larger than under the brief alone, persists under temperature-zero re-probing, and stays positive without typed memory extraction in exploratory tests. Matched solo generation reproduces part of it, and social interaction remains highest. Across five more model variants, every scenario-averaged interaction contrast is positive. Each interacting population is therefore one replicate, and treating its agents as independent requires paired no-interaction controls. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/koanatakiyo/SocCogEval.

papers.title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning
papers.summary: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.

papers.title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
papers.summary: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

papers.title: ARRANGE: Agentic Skills for Layering Vocals
papers.summary: Adding a singing voice to an existing piano recording requires decisions about melody, syllable placement, pronunciation, timing, and vocal register. ARRANGE organizes this work as a sequence of agent skills with readable intermediate artifacts and composer approval checkpoints. An LLM translates instructions in plain English, notes played on a keyboard, and vocal references into local edits; deterministic scripts validate and apply those edits before open audio models render the result. The Score Canvas makes note, syllable, and pronunciation decisions inspectable and editable. In a benchmark of 16 revision requests, three draws per request, and five LLMs, typed edits achieved exact-change correctness of 0.83-0.98, compared with 0.33-0.69 for whole-plan rewriting without ARRANGE instructions. A separate score-editing benchmark and a first-person worked example examine the interaction between representations and corrections. Author listening evaluations further explore voice transfer and register selection, including 185 listening presentations across eight copied voices. These evaluations support the value of constrained editing and expose limits of both model execution and listening measures. The contribution is an interaction architecture for retaining musical decisions through inspectable intermediate representations, rather than a new singing model or evidence of general usability.

papers.title: Beyond Evidence Coverage: Encoding-Time Access in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Cache-sharing multi-agent systems can retain every evidence token's representation while preventing cross-worker access during encoding. We test whether this coverage recovers joint-encoding quality using attention masks over two logical workers in frozen Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models. Tokens, positions, and answer-time access remain fixed within comparisons. We evaluate 200 two-hop MuSiQue-Ans questions and 200 selected HotpotQA bridge questions. In data-layout seed 0, averaged across models, blocking access costs 5.6 and 6.8 F1 points relative to full access on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, respectively. Exposing the earlier worker's supporting paragraph improves F1 over blocked access by 7.6 and 6.7 points; equal-token non-support access provides no detectable average gain. With model weights and greedy decoding fixed, we vary distractor layouts using five data-layout seeds per dataset for Qwen3-8B and three for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Supporting-paragraph access has higher mean F1 than blocked and equal-token non-support access in every evaluated data-layout seed. Supporting access can also outperform full access, but its advantage depends on the model, dataset, and layout. Oracle support labels isolate access from selection error; the study does not evaluate a deployable selector. Complete evidence coverage at answer time therefore does not guarantee joint-encoding quality: which supporting facts can interact during encoding matters.

papers.title: Factory-simulator: A process-oriented environment for evaluating manufacturing decisions against optimisation-based references
papers.summary: Motivated by discussions with an electronics contract manufacturer about decision support, Factory-simulator provides a deterministic manufacturing environment for controlled research on the business performance of large language model-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS). Equal delivery performance can arise from decisions with different financial consequences, complicating evaluation through delivery metrics alone. Its process-oriented model connects procurement and production decisions to order fulfilment and factory finances. Seeded worlds and recorded actions support replay and branching from a shared history to examine alternative decisions and their downstream consequences. Linear and mixed-integer programming models generate profit-oriented reference decisions. Observation-limited comparators use disclosed information; full-foresight references use future events for diagnostic comparison. Controlled examples show equal delivery performance with different profit under the same information and distinguish delivery penalties from deferred payment. Verification includes material and financial balances, replay and forks, and a small allocation instance in which the tested optimisation-based controllers attain an analytically established optimum. An external three-role LLM-MAS client completed four illustrative runs comprising 159 periods, with reconciled balances and exact replay of recorded actions. Matched-world rolling comparisons contextualise the financial outcomes, while full-foresight results provide heuristic reference points rather than certified optima. The software enables researchers to investigate how agent organisation and information access affect business outcomes, including whether distributing procurement and production responsibilities changes profit relative to a centralised controller.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. We designed a series of agents with systematically varying risk preferences and paired them in a repeated joint decision-making task previously conducted with humans. Like humans, agents converged toward their partners' choices. However, similar aggregate behavior arose from different dynamics: agents showed little evidence of reciprocal adjustment, tended to weigh rewards more, and their responsibility attribution was decoupled from compromise. Similarly, while they showed bias in their responsibility attribution, the outcome's valence shaped the attribution differently than in humans. Our results reveal important differences between human--human and agent--agent joint decision-making, demonstrating that similar social outcomes can emerge from different social dynamics and reasoning.

papers.title: Who Speaks for the Water? Simulating Discursive Closure and Power Asymmetries in Hydrosocial Governance
papers.summary: Water governance conflicts stem not only from material scarcity, but from power asymmetries, institutional distrust, and the discursive frameworks through which actors assign meaning to water, infrastructure, and legitimate authority. Conventional simulation tools represent these dynamics via numerical opinion variables, missing the argumentative and narrative dimensions structuring real deliberation in hydrosocial territories. We present the Hydrosocial Agent-Based Model with Large Language Models (HSABM-LLM), a hybrid framework enabling heterogeneous agents to generate, evaluate, and adapt natural language arguments conditioned on institutional roles, interaction histories, and territorial context. Grounded in semi-structured interviews, a water-user survey, and 456 press and official documents from the Longaví River sub-basin (Maule Region, Chile), the model simulates deliberation over a contested large-scale reservoir proposal across four experimental scenarios. Opinion convergence toward unanimous opposition emerged within 7-14 months, operating through discursive closure driven by distributive equity and water security framings rather than argumentative dominance. Governance actors accelerated convergence by activating pre-existing institutional distrust rather than direct persuasion, while peer-based smallholder interactions drove 77-79% of all opinion changes. The formal authority of state institutions proved structurally decoupled from deliberative influence, revealing a legitimacy deficit that formal inclusion alone cannot resolve. These findings suggest participatory governance design must attend to the discursive conditions under which institutional actors enter deliberative spaces, rather than assuming inclusion is inherently consensus-building. HSABM-LLM offers a novel platform for integrating political ecology insights into computational social science.

papers.title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.

papers.title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

papers.title: MACE: Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation of Frozen Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: In plant phenotyping, crop disease diagnosis has traditionally relied on expert assessment of visible symptoms and on models tailored to specific crops or diseases, and both are difficult to scale across field conditions. Recent methods provide frozen vision-language models with source-grounded knowledge bases that summarize the typical symptoms of each disease but describe little of how symptoms vary across individual cases. We introduce MACE (Memory-Augmented Crop-Disease Evaluation), a training-free method that supplements the knowledge base with a memory of symptom descriptions paired with known disease labels. MACE matches a description of the query image against this memory and retrieves only text descriptions and disease labels, so the query is the only image that the diagnosis model sees. Across ten crops, MACE with Claude Sonnet 5.5 improved accuracy over the knowledge-base baseline from 42.8% to 62.2% in distribution and from 50.7% to 57.0% on held-out image collections. Retrieved disease labels accounted for most of the gain, and adding the corresponding text descriptions improved in-distribution accuracy by about six percentage points.

papers.title: Digital Twins for Multi-Agent Systems: When to Trust, What to Change
papers.summary: Digital twins of agent networks need to flag unreliable forecasts and help users choose interventions. Both decisions depend on what happens over several steps: an error can spread through the network, and an edit whose trajectory is easy to predict may still yield a poor collective outcome. We ask when information about error propagation improves failure detection and whether a learned twin can select effective network edits despite imperfect forecasts. We propose Propagation-Aware Validation for Networked Digital Twins (PAV-Twin). Its monitor combines Jacobian-based propagation features with recent errors and ensemble disagreement to estimate the risk that a forecast exceeds an error threshold. Its planner simulates each candidate edit and ranks the edits by their predicted collective outcomes. In simulations, the monitor gained 0.13 in area under the precision-recall curve on larger oscillator networks with familiar topologies and 0.09 on larger networks with held-out topologies, relative to a graph baseline without propagation features. Gains were small in contractive consensus. Giving the graph baseline the same features narrowed the gap. In a separate planning study, ensemble simulation recovered about 99% of the possible improvement over random intervention selection in oscillators and nearly all of it in consensus. With a simplified oscillator twin, selecting by predicted outcome also gave lower regret than selecting by trajectory fidelity. These results show when propagation features help flag unreliable forecasts and why the quality of intervention choices should be measured directly.

papers.title: How a Prediction Dies: A Challenge-Driven, Rule-Bound Self-Refutation in an LLM Agent Society
papers.summary: Persistent societies of large language model agents now make empirical claims about their own collective behaviour, yet the fate of such claims is rarely observable. We document one claim, from registration to death, on AITRAP, a multi-agent platform whose public, append-only ledger records every action. The claim (0495d171, registered 19 October 2026) asserted that a majority of bridges between problem domains would remain attached to a single exploration lineage. Three community challenges forced its judgment criterion through four versions, from an ambiguous statement to an executable protocol with a fixed threshold, a minimum-frame-size gate, and a baseline calibration gate. When the first frame with at least 20 bridges arrived, support stood at 9 of 79 (11.4%; Wilson 95% CI [6.1%, 20.3%]); the author, bound by the registered clause, refuted the claim and relinquished the associated stake. Three findings emerge. The criterion became executable only under community pressure, which we document version by version. The calibration gate caught a fault in the author's own recalculation that would otherwise have published a spuriously perfect 0/79 result. The failure itself traces to a denominator that grew 8.8-fold in five days while the numerator grew 1.8-fold, coinciding with a change in platform incentives; we report this mechanism as a hypothesis, not a rescuing condition. A claim whose termination is carried out exactly as written carries more evidential weight than one that survives, and this case provides initial empirical grounds for treating voluntary self-refutation as a candidate indicator of epistemic accountability in incentive-coupled agent societies.
